title: Ciabatta workflow
description: A named, described, owned set of steps — build, test, lint, deploy, whatever the repo agrees on. Lives at .ciabatta/workflows/<name>.yaml; the workflow's name is the filename.

description.description: What running this workflow accomplishes. `ciabatta list` prints it.

owner.description: Who owns it — a name, handle, or team. Falls back to the sub-workspace's owner.

needs.description: Workflows in OTHER sub-workspaces that must finish first, on top of whatever `workspace.depends_on` already declares. A step's own `needs` names steps in this file; cross-package dependencies belong here.

requires.description: Tools this workflow needs on PATH, applied to all of its steps. Missing ones are reported before anything runs, with the install command from the root's `toolchain:` section.

env_file.description: .env file path(s) relative to the sub-workspace, sourced before the graph runs.

REQUIRED_ENV.description: Variables that must be set and non-empty, or the run is refused up front.

env.description: Environment variables applied to every step of this workflow.

tags.description: Free-form labels for search and for `--filter tag:<name>`. Every step in this workflow inherits them.

cache.description: What this workflow's builds read and write. It lives here rather than in ciabatta.yaml because the files a `build` reads are not the files a `test` reads. The cache *server* stays in ciabatta.yaml.

steps.description: The steps themselves. Order in the file doesn't matter — `needs` does.

background.description: Workflows that must be RUNNING for this one to finish: a mock API the integration tests call, a database container, a bundler in watch mode. Named the same way `needs` names things — "<member>" for that sub-workspace's workflow of this name, "<member>:<workflow>" for a specific one — because they are the same kind of thing: a target that already exists, declared once, in its own package. The only difference from `needs` is that a `needs` target is waited for and a `background` target is merely started: its steps gate nothing, so no mistake in one can hold a build up, and they are stopped again once every stage has succeeded or failed. That lifetime is the whole difference from a step with `persistent: true`, which the daemon keeps alive on purpose so a `dev` workflow leaves you a server to work against.
